source.facts: Confirmed by Winston (Nov 2026): co-founder and only designer; the other seven were developers; he made product calls and handed off designs; Nov 2022 – Jan 2025; A2–A4 sections are closest to v1.0 (iOS, Nov 2024; also on Android); live timing shipped and detected delays automatically from posted results; tournament mode exists because you don't need those features outside an event, other features help you find teams and tournaments then, and its UI is built for the fast-paced tournament environment (own experience + tester input); your own next match leads with the time because time is what you act on (own experience competing + user/team feedback); the 2023 plan's organizer portal, chatbot and web app gave way to priorities; the ScoutSheet tab (A5) shipped in a later update; TeamSync, Groups and the new onboarding (A5/R1/R2) were designed but not shipped; feedback after launch led to fixes only; 4,000+ accounts; 4.8-star rating; '3x faster' came from automated tests clicking through competitor apps vs Elapse to reach the same data. Takeaways he chose: design for the moment; ship the core first; live data needs honest states. Follow-up: live timing was in v1.0; tournament mode switches off after the event; some scouting (robot specs on the team sheet) was in v1.0. Depth round: next-match card is pale red or blue by your alliance; pale cyan is the brand colour, calm in a loud venue; big numbers follow the info hierarchy, how teams talk, anchor dense screens; cards are only tinted if you were in the match, otherwise grey, and 'You won!' speaks to the user; alliance colours = VEX convention, know your side, less labelling; schedule rows: match number left and large, all four teams grouped on one side, time and field out of the middle; users said it helped them find matches a lot easier. Title: Winston asked for 'Elapse App' (Nov 2026); the slug stays as is. Copy round (Nov 2026): each case ends with a short Summary. Layout (Nov 2026): per Winston's V3 design, the How might we statement is the heading of the first content section, titled 'Problem Statement'; the summary field is a short line on what he did. The summary line never says “I”; it starts with a verb ending in -ing (Nov 2026).

fields.title: Elapse App
fields.description: A tournament companion for VEX Robotics teams: next match, live schedule and scouting. 4,000+ accounts.
fields.intro: I co-founded Elapse, an app that shows VEX Robotics teams their next match, a live schedule and scouting. I was the only designer, working with seven developers.
fields.summary: Co-founding Elapse and designing it end to end, from your next match to a mode for tournament day.
fields.overview: I made product calls and handed off designs to the developers. Elapse launched on iOS in November 2024 and is also on Android.

hero.alt: An iPhone showing an early Elapse home design: the Q23 next match card with alliance teams, field and time

sections.title: Problem Statement
sections.heading: How might we help robotics teams know when and where their next match is, even when the schedule runs late?
content: I competed in VEX Robotics for four years. At tournaments, I ran into three problems:

bullets: The official schedule app took several taps and spread information across screens.
Schedules weren’t updated when matches ran late.
Announcements over the mic were easy to miss.

sections.title: Plan vs. release
sections.heading: From plan to release
content: The 2023 plan was bigger than what we launched. We cut it back to focus on what teams needed most.

notes.text: Robot specs on each team’s sheet
ScoutSheet tab on each team’s page
An organizer portal for delays and announcements
A web app for phones, tablets and computers

sections.title: Next match
sections.heading: Your next match comes first
content: On your own next match, the time and “In X minutes” come first. Other matches lead with the match number.

bullets: **Why time first:** time is what you act on.
**Where it came from:** my own time competing, plus user and team feedback.

content.alt: Three iPhones: the Elapse home with a next match card, your next match leading with the time, and another match leading with the match number
content.caption: Home, your next match (time first), another match (number first).

bullets: **Your next-match card takes your alliance’s colour,** pale red or blue, so you know your side at a glance.
**Team numbers are red or blue** too. It’s the VEX convention, and it saves extra labels.
**Big numbers follow the hierarchy,** so what matters most reads at a glance. Match and team numbers are also how teams talk, and they anchor screens full of small stats.
**The pale cyan is Elapse’s brand colour.** It keeps things calm in a loud venue.

content.alt: A close-up of the Elapse next match card in pale red: 3:25PM, In 5 minutes, match Q23 on field Inspire
content.caption: Your next match, in your alliance’s colour.

sections.title: Schedule
sections.heading: A schedule you can scan
content: Other apps put the time and field in the middle of each row, with each alliance’s teams on either side. But competitors mostly scroll fast, looking for a match number or a team.

bullets: **The match number sits on the left, large,** since that’s what people look for most.
**All four teams sit together on one side,** so you can scan them at once instead of reading down blue, then going back up for red.
**Time and field moved out of the middle.**

content: People using the app said it made finding matches a lot easier.

content.alt: A close-up of Elapse schedule rows: large match numbers on the left, time and score next to them, and all four team numbers grouped on the right
content.caption: Match numbers on the left, all four teams together.

sections.title: Live timing
sections.heading: Delays you can see
content: Matches often run late. Live timing worked out delays from posted match results and updated the schedule automatically.
Instead of quietly changing the time, the app shows the new time with “Delayed - originally …”, and finished matches show how late they started.
Match cards are only tinted when your team played. Every other match stays grey, and your own results speak to you: “You won!”.

content.alt: Two Elapse match cards side by side: a light blue You won! card for a match your team played, and a grey card for a match it didn’t
content.caption: Tinted when your team played, grey when it didn’t.

content.alt: Two iPhones: Your Next Match with “Delayed - originally” under the new time, and a finished match that started 3 minutes late
content.caption: A delayed match, and a finished one that started late.

sections.title: Tournament mode
sections.heading: A mode for tournament day
content: Tournament mode is for when you’re at an event. You turn it on from the home screen, and it switches off after the event.

bullets: **You don’t need it outside an event.** Other features help you find teams and tournaments then.
**Its UI is built for a fast-paced day** at the event.
**It came from my own experience** and from testers.

content.alt: Three iPhones: the Elapse home with a Tournament Mode button, then the Schedule and Rankings tabs inside tournament mode
content.caption: Turning it on from home, then Schedule and Rankings inside the mode.

sections.title: Outcome
sections.heading: After launch
content: In our automated tests, which clicked through competitor apps and Elapse to reach the same data, Elapse was 3x faster. After launch, feedback led to fixes.
The ScoutSheet tab on each team’s page came in a later update.

content.alt: Two iPhones: an Elapse team page with an empty Scoutsheet tab, and a filled ScoutSheet
content.caption: A team’s ScoutSheet, empty and filled.

bullets: **Design for the moment.** Tournament day leaves little attention. The next match has to be readable at a glance.
**Ship the core first.** Leaving the portal and chatbot out let us release what teams needed.
**Live data needs honest states.** Show a delay next to the original time instead of hiding it.

content: Elapse started from problems I ran into while competing. The official app spread the schedule across screens, and schedules didn’t update when matches ran late. I was co-founder and the only designer, working with seven developers. I designed an app that puts your next match first, updates the schedule when matches run late, and has a mode built for tournament day.
It launched on iOS in November 2024, is also on Android, and has 4,000+ accounts and a 4.8-star rating.
